title: Problem 06
markdown:
Find all positive real numbers $c$ satisfying

$$\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{1}{n + kc} = \frac{1}{c}.$$

### Solution (adapted from the official solution)
The unique solution is $c = e - 1$.

Rewrite the sum by factoring out $1/n$:

$$\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{1}{n + kc} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{1}{1 + c(k/n)}.$$

This is a Riemann sum for the continuous function $f(x) = \frac{1}{1 + cx}$ on the interval $[0, 1]$ with sample points $x_k = k/n$ and step size $\Delta x = 1/n$.

Taking the limit as $n \to \infty$:

$$\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{1}{n + kc} = \int_0^1 \frac{1}{1 + cx} \, dx = \left[ \frac{1}{c} \ln(1 + cx) \right]_0^1 = \frac{1}{c} \ln(1 + c).$$

We are given that this limit equals $\frac{1}{c}$:

$$\frac{1}{c} \ln(1 + c) = \frac{1}{c}.$$

Since $c > 0$, multiply by $c$:

$$\ln(1 + c) = 1 \implies 1 + c = e \implies c = e - 1.$$

### Conceptual Explanation
Recognizing the sum as a Riemann sum for $\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{1+cx} = \frac{1}{c}\ln(1+c)$ equates $\frac{1}{c}\ln(1+c) = \frac{1}{c}$, which simplifies to $\ln(1+c) = 1 \implies c = e - 1$.

### Key Technique
Riemann sum recognition and definite integration of rational functions.
